```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
root <- rprojroot::find_root(rprojroot::has_file("DESCRIPTION"))
res_dir <- file.path(root, "analysis", "results")
fig_dir <- file.path(root, "analysis", "figures")

cov <- read.csv(file.path(res_dir, "coverage-performance.csv"))
cvp <- read.csv(file.path(res_dir, "cv-selection-performance.csv"))
sel <- read.csv(file.path(res_dir, "cv-selection-rates.csv"))
prov_cov <- readLines(file.path(res_dir, "coverage-provenance.txt"))
prov_cv <- readLines(file.path(res_dir, "cv-selection-provenance.txt"))
prov <- function(lines, key) sub(paste0("^", key, ": "), "", grep(paste0("^", key, ":"), lines, value = TRUE))

pct <- function(x, d = 1) sprintf(paste0("%.", d, "f%%"), 100 * x)
get_cov <- function(n, sigma, method, measure = "coverage") {
  cov[cov$n == n & cov$sigma == sigma & cov$method == method &
        cov$measure == measure, ]
}
get_cv <- function(n, p, beta, method, aggregation = "pooled",
                   measure = "bias") {
  cvp[cvp$n == n & cvp$p == p & cvp$beta == beta & cvp$method == method &
        cvp$aggregation == aggregation & cvp$measure == measure, ]
}
nested_pooled_bias <- cvp[cvp$measure == "bias" & cvp$method == "nested" &
                            cvp$aggregation == "pooled", ]
fmt <- function(row, d = 3) sprintf("%.*f (MCSE %.*f)", d, row$estimate, d, row$mcse)
max_mcse_cov <- max(cov$mcse[cov$measure == "coverage"])
```

# Abstract {-}

We report two Monte Carlo experiments, designed and reported according to the
ADEMP framework [@morris2019], using the `RDataScienceCompendium` R package.
**Study 1** compares five nominal 95% confidence intervals for the mean of
log-normal data. The Student $t$ interval had the best coverage for mild to
moderate skew at every sample size studied. With strong skew
($\sigma = 1$), all intervals under-covered: at $n = 10$ coverage ranged
from `r pct(min(cov$estimate[cov$measure == "coverage" & cov$n == 10 & cov$sigma == 1]))`
(basic bootstrap) to
`r pct(max(cov$estimate[cov$measure == "coverage" & cov$n == 10 & cov$sigma == 1]))`.
The BCa interval was the best or joint-best bootstrap method in every
scenario with strong skew. **Study 2** shows that reporting the cross-validated error of the
best-performing candidate model is optimistically biased. The bias was
largest with small samples and many candidates: at $n = 50$ with 25 noise
candidates, the true RMSE was understated by
`r sprintf("%.3f", -get_cv(50, 25, 0, "naive", "fold")$estimate)` on average. Nested cross-validation removed
the selection bias, but only when the RMSE was computed from the pooled
out-of-fold predictions. Averaging per-fold RMSEs, which is common practice,
left a residual optimism of up to
`r sprintf("%.3f", -min(cvp$estimate[cvp$measure == "bias" & cvp$method == "nested" & cvp$aggregation == "fold"]))`
caused by Jensen's inequality. All results carry
Monte Carlo standard errors (MCSEs) and can be regenerated with a single
command.

# Introduction

Resampling methods are often recommended because they relax distributional
assumptions. Whether they deliver on this promise at the sample sizes seen in
practice is an empirical question, and simulation studies are the standard
tool for answering it. Simulation studies are experiments, however, and their
conclusions are only as reliable as their design and their quantification of
Monte Carlo error [@morris2019].

We study two questions that come up routinely in applied work:

1. Do bootstrap confidence intervals for a mean improve on the $t$ interval
   when the data are skewed and $n$ is small [@efron1987; @davison1997]?
2. How optimistic is it to report the cross-validation (CV) error of the
   model that was *chosen* by that same CV, and does nested CV fix this
   [@varma2006; @cawley2010]?

# Methods

All computations use the `RDataScienceCompendium` package (version
`r prov(prov_cov, "package_version")`). Each (scenario, replicate) pair has
its own L'Ecuyer-CMRG random-number stream [@lecuyer2002], so results do not
depend on how many parallel workers are used. The seeds and run times are
listed in the provenance files in `analysis/results/`.

## Study 1: interval coverage under skewness

| ADEMP | Specification |
|---|---|
| **Aims** | Compare coverage and width of five nominal 95% intervals for a mean. |
| **Data-generating mechanisms** | $X_i \sim \mathrm{LogNormal}(0, \sigma^2)$, $n \in \{10, 20, 40, 80\}$, $\sigma \in \{0.25, 0.5, 1\}$ (skewness 0.78, 1.75, 6.18); full factorial, 12 scenarios. |
| **Estimand** | $\theta = E[X] = \exp(\sigma^2/2)$. |
| **Methods** | Student $t$; nonparametric bootstrap percentile, basic, normal and BCa intervals with $R = 1999$ resamples. |
| **Performance measures** | Coverage (primary), bias-eliminated coverage, mean width. |
| **Replicates** | `r prov(prov_cov, "n_sim")` per scenario, so that coverage MCSE $\le 0.31$ percentage points near 95%. The largest observed coverage MCSE was `r sprintf("%.2f", 100 * max_mcse_cov)` points. |

## Study 2: optimism after model selection by cross-validation

| ADEMP | Specification |
|---|---|
| **Aims** | Quantify the bias of two estimators of the prediction error of a "select by CV, then refit" procedure. |
| **Data-generating mechanisms** | $p$ independent $N(0,1)$ candidate predictors; $y = \beta x_1 + \varepsilon$, $\varepsilon \sim N(0,1)$; $n \in \{50, 200\}$, $p \in \{5, 25\}$, $\beta \in \{0, 0.5\}$; 8 scenarios. |
| **Estimand** | RMSE of the final (selected and refitted) model on new data, evaluated on an independent test set of 10,000 observations. |
| **Methods** | *Naive*: the minimum over candidates of the 5-fold CV RMSE. *Nested*: 5 $\times$ 5 nested CV. Each is computed in two ways: by averaging the per-fold RMSEs (*fold*), and from the pooled out-of-fold predictions (*pooled*). Candidates are the $p$ single-predictor linear models. |
| **Performance measures** | Bias (primary), empirical SE and MSE of each estimator. |
| **Replicates** | `r prov(prov_cv, "n_sim")` per scenario. |

Nested CV estimates the error of the procedure when it is trained on 80% of
the data. It is therefore expected to be slightly *pessimistic* about a
model trained on all $n$ observations. We added the pooled variants after a
pilot run showed nested CV to be unexpectedly *optimistic*. Our hypothesis
was that averaging square roots of per-fold mean squared errors is biased
downwards when test folds are small, since
$E[\sqrt{\widehat{\mathrm{MSE}}}] \le \sqrt{E[\widehat{\mathrm{MSE}}]}$.
The pooled variants test this hypothesis directly.

# Results

No replicate failed in either study
(`r prov(prov_cov, "failed_replicates")` and
`r prov(prov_cv, "failed_replicates")` failures).

## Study 1

```{r fig-coverage, fig.cap = "Figure 1. Coverage of nominal 95% intervals for a log-normal mean. Bars are ±1.96 MCSE."}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(fig_dir, "coverage.png"))
```

```{r tab-coverage}
tab <- cov[cov$measure == "coverage", c("sigma", "n", "method", "estimate", "mcse")]
tab$value <- sprintf("%.1f (%.1f)", 100 * tab$estimate, 100 * tab$mcse)
wide <- reshape(tab[, c("sigma", "n", "method", "value")],
                idvar = c("sigma", "n"), timevar = "method",
                direction = "wide")
names(wide) <- sub("^value\\.", "", names(wide))
wide <- wide[order(wide$sigma, wide$n), c("sigma", "n", "t", "bca",
                                           "percentile", "normal", "basic")]
knitr::kable(wide, row.names = FALSE,
             caption = "Table 1. Coverage, % (MCSE), of nominal 95% intervals.")
```

At $\sigma = 0.25$ and $n = 10$, the $t$ interval achieved
`r pct(get_cov(10, 0.25, "t")$estimate)` coverage. Every bootstrap interval
stayed below `r pct(max(sapply(c("bca", "percentile", "normal", "basic"), function(m) get_cov(10, 0.25, m)$estimate)))`.
The bootstrap intervals are too narrow in small samples, partly because
they use the plug-in variance, which divides by $n$ rather than $n-1$
[@davison1997]. Under strong skew ($\sigma = 1$) the ordering changes with
$n$. At $n = 10$ the $t$ interval
(`r pct(get_cov(10, 1, "t")$estimate)`) and BCa
(`r pct(get_cov(10, 1, "bca")$estimate)`) are both far from nominal. At
$n = 80$ BCa reaches `r pct(get_cov(80, 1, "bca")$estimate)` compared with
`r pct(get_cov(80, 1, "t")$estimate)` for $t$. The basic interval was the
worst or tied for worst in every scenario with $\sigma \ge 0.5$.

```{r tab-width}
w <- cov[cov$measure == "mean_width" & cov$n == 20, c("sigma", "method", "estimate")]
w$estimate <- sprintf("%.3f", w$estimate)
ww <- reshape(w, idvar = "sigma", timevar = "method", direction = "wide")
names(ww) <- sub("^estimate\\.", "", names(ww))
knitr::kable(ww[, c("sigma", "t", "bca", "percentile", "normal", "basic")],
             row.names = FALSE,
             caption = "Table 2. Mean interval width at n = 20.")
```

## Study 2

```{r fig-cv, fig.cap = "Figure 2. Bias of the naive and nested CV estimates of the final model's RMSE. Bars are ±1.96 MCSE."}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(fig_dir, "cv-bias.png"))
```

```{r tab-cv}
b <- cvp[cvp$measure == "bias", ]
b$key <- paste(b$method, b$aggregation, sep = ", ")
b$value <- sprintf("%+.3f (%.3f)", b$estimate, b$mcse)
bw <- reshape(b[, c("beta", "n", "p", "key", "value")],
              idvar = c("beta", "n", "p"), timevar = "key",
              direction = "wide")
names(bw) <- sub("^value\\.", "", names(bw))
bw <- merge(bw, sel, by = c("n", "p", "beta"))
bw$selected_true_predictor <- ifelse(bw$beta == 0, "—",
                                     pct(bw$selected_true_predictor, 0))
bw <- bw[order(bw$beta, bw$p, bw$n),
         c("beta", "n", "p", "naive, fold", "naive, pooled", "nested, fold",
           "nested, pooled", "selected_true_predictor")]
names(bw)[8] <- "P(select x1)"
knitr::kable(bw, row.names = FALSE,
             caption = "Table 3. Bias (MCSE) of CV estimates of the final model's RMSE, and how often the true predictor was selected.")
```

**Selection bias.** The naive estimate was optimistic in every scenario
where the choice among candidates was not obvious, under both aggregations.
Its bias grew with the number of candidates and shrank with $n$. Under the
null, pooled naive bias went from
`r fmt(get_cv(200, 5, 0, "naive"))` at $n = 200, p = 5$ to
`r fmt(get_cv(50, 25, 0, "naive"))` at $n = 50, p = 25$. When a real signal
was present and $n = 200$, the true predictor was always selected and the
optimism essentially vanished (`r fmt(get_cv(200, 25, 0.5, "naive"))`).

**Aggregation bias.** The fold-averaged nested estimate was also optimistic,
for example `r fmt(get_cv(50, 5, 0, "nested", "fold"))` at $n = 50, p = 5$.
Pooling removed this bias
(`r fmt(get_cv(50, 5, 0, "nested", "pooled"))`). This is consistent with it being an
artefact of averaging per-fold RMSEs and not a failure of nested CV. With
pooling, nested CV had `r sum(abs(nested_pooled_bias$estimate) < 2 * nested_pooled_bias$mcse)`
of `r nrow(nested_pooled_bias)` biases within 2 MCSE of zero. The
exceptions were small and *positive*, at most
`r sprintf("%+.3f", max(nested_pooled_bias$estimate))`. That is the
expected pessimism from training on 80% of the data, and it is largest
when $n = 50$ and there are many candidates to choose from.

# Discussion

In Study 1 the bootstrap offered no advantage over the $t$ interval for the
mean at small $n$ and moderate skew. For strongly skewed data, BCa was the
best bootstrap interval and overtook $t$ as $n$ grew. No method was
satisfactory at $n = 10$ with heavy skew. This agrees with the theoretical
second-order accuracy of BCa, and with its known small-sample
narrowness [@efron1987; @davison1997]. The practical lesson is to present
small-sample intervals for skewed data with appropriate caution, not to
choose the bootstrap by default.

Study 2 puts numbers on a well-known pitfall. Selecting among only 25
single-variable models is enough to make naive CV understate prediction
error by several percent when $n = 50$. Nested CV is the remedy
[@varma2006; @cawley2010], but the study also exposed a second, less
familiar source of optimism. Averaging per-fold RMSEs is biased
downwards when test folds are small, and at $n = 50$ this bias was about as
large as the selection bias that nested CV is meant to remove. Computing
non-linear metrics such as the RMSE from the pooled out-of-fold predictions
[@forman2010] avoids the problem. The `RDataScienceCompendium` functions
`cross_validate()` and `nested_cv()` now report both versions. Once pooled,
nested CV's remaining bias is small and conservative.

**Limitations.** Study 1 considers only log-normal data and the mean;
heavier tails or other statistics may favour different methods. Study 2
uses a simple class of candidate models and a single choice of fold counts.
Both designs are easy to extend with the scripts provided.

# Reproducibility {-}

From the repository root:

```sh
make analysis   # install package, run both studies, draw figures, render paper
```

The studies used a machine with
`r sub(" \\(.*", "", prov(prov_cov, "backend"))` backend and took
`r prov(prov_cov, "elapsed_seconds")` s (Study 1) and
`r prov(prov_cv, "elapsed_seconds")` s (Study 2) of wall-clock time on
`r prov(prov_cov, "platform")` running `r prov(prov_cov, "r_version")`.
Because every replicate has its own random-number stream, the numbers in
this paper are reproduced exactly with any number of workers
(`RDSC_WORKERS=1` for a sequential run).
